spec.cue: Mostly blue-green and dim, with little colour and soft detail, as a whale or seal sees it.

cpd.note: the middle of the cetacean and seal sharpness records, with the app's pick of 3.5

gain.note: the brightening is the app's pick; the records show a reflecting layer but give no dim-light ratio

BEE_OR_MONO.note: a two-channel reading that stands in for the records, which show only one cone class

rows: Most of these animals have one kind of cone, so they see little or no colour. Their picture is mostly in shades of blue-green and grey.
A bottlenose dolphin, a Bryde's whale and a harbour seal resolve detail to a rough fraction of a person's. We soften the picture to about 3.5 cycles per degree.
Cetaceans and seals have a reflecting layer behind the retina, so dim light is brightened a little. The amount of brightening is the app's own choice.
The colour mapping, the blur and the brightness are the app's own choices. They lean on the records above but are not read from any one animal.

claims.how: The value 3.5 lies between the cited cetacean and seal records (3.3 to 11.5 cycles per degree), and the app chose the point.

quotes.quote: we estimated the peak anatomical spatial resolving power in water to be 4.8 cycles/degree and 3.3 cycles/degree in the Bryde's whale and the humpback whale, respectively
we estimated the peak anatomical spatial resolving power in water to be 4.8 cycles/degree and 3.3 cycles/degree in the Bryde's whale and the humpback whale, respectively
Retinal resolution was calculated as 11.5 cycles/deg under water and 8.7 cycles/deg in air
The resolving power in the right eyes of two individuals was 2.60 and 2.64 cycles per degree.
Visual acuity was estimated at 3.95 cycles per degree (CPD)
we here demonstrate an absence of S-cones in the retinae of all whales and seals studied
These marine mammals have only L-cones (cone monochromacy) and hence are essentially colour-blind.
since harbor seals possess only one cone type
Since their retina seems to contain only L-opsins and rods (Jacobs 2009; Springer et al. 2016) implying colorblindness
